body:
Who is responsible for nuclear safety?

The organization operating a nuclear installation has the primary responsibility for safety. It must maintain safe operating conditions, inspect and test equipment, train personnel, follow approved procedures, monitor radiation and prepare for emergencies.

A regulatory authority provides independent safety oversight through requirements, reviews, permissions, inspections and enforcement. The existence of a regulator does not transfer the operator's day-to-day safety responsibility to the regulator.

The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board

India's Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) was constituted on 15 November 1983 under powers provided by the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. Its principal role is to protect people and the environment from undue risks associated with nuclear energy and ionizing radiation.

AERB establishes safety requirements, evaluates applications for regulatory consent, reviews safety arrangements, conducts inspections and takes appropriate regulatory action. Its regulatory work covers stages such as siting, construction, commissioning, operation and decommissioning, according to the applicable requirements.

The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) operates India's commercial nuclear power stations. The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) undertakes nuclear research and develops technologies, including radioactive-waste management technologies. These functions differ from AERB's regulatory role.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) develops international safety standards and provides guidance, reviews and assistance to member countries. It is not the routine licensing authority for an Indian nuclear power station; national regulatory authority remains central to licensing and enforcement.

Emergency planning must extend beyond the plant

Preparedness is required even when preventive systems are extensive. Emergency plans identify foreseeable hazards, responsibilities, communication channels, monitoring arrangements and protective measures before an actual emergency occurs.

Emergency categoryArea of concernPrincipal response
Plant emergencyEmergency conditions within a plant or facilityPlant personnel respond under the approved plant plan.
Site emergencyConditions requiring response across the nuclear siteSite management coordinates protective actions across affected facilities.
Off-site emergencyPotential radiological consequences beyond the siteDistrict and other public authorities coordinate off-site protection with the facility.

The category reflects the nature and potential consequences of the event. Declaration of an off-site emergency does not necessarily mean that a large radioactive release has already occurred; preventive protective action may be required because a significant release is possible.

Plant and site emergency arrangements are subject to AERB regulatory review, approval and requirements. Off-site arrangements involve the facility operator and state or district authorities, with approval by the relevant state or district authorities and district-level coordination under applicable plans.

Protective measures during a radiological emergency

Authorities assess the event using radiation monitoring, weather information, expected exposure pathways and the seriousness of the hazard. Depending on the circumstances, responses may include:

  • Alerting relevant emergency services and informing potentially affected people.
  • Restricting entry to affected areas and controlling access.
  • Advising sheltering indoors or evacuation when justified by the situation.
  • Providing medical assessment and decontamination where necessary.
  • Using stable iodine prophylaxis only when specifically advised by competent public-health authorities for a relevant radioactive-iodine exposure risk.
  • Monitoring food, water and the environment, followed by appropriate recovery measures.

Emergency exercises test whether personnel, equipment, communications and public authorities can work together as intended. A plan that exists only on paper is not sufficient preparation.

Safety culture: the human part of nuclear protection

Safety culture consists of the attitudes and practices through which individuals and organizations give safety the priority it requires. It includes competent training, accurate records, questioning unexpected readings, reporting errors and near misses, observing operating limits and learning from events.

Good safety culture does not treat an alarm or unusual condition as unimportant merely because no accident has occurred previously. Personnel must be able to raise concerns, and managers must ensure that production objectives do not override necessary safety measures.

Prelims focus

  • AERB was constituted on 15 November 1983 under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962.
  • The operator retains primary responsibility for installation safety.
  • AERB regulates; NPCIL operates commercial nuclear power stations.
  • Emergency categories include plant, site and off-site emergencies.
  • Safety culture includes reporting problems, learning from experience and following safety requirements.
  • Trap: The IAEA develops international standards but does not ordinarily issue Indian nuclear-plant operating licences.

[Sources: IAEA, Fundamental Safety Principles, SF-1, Principles 1, 2, 8 and 9; IAEA, Safety of Nuclear Power Plants: Design, SSR-2/1 (Rev. 1), safety management requirements (consulted 16 November 2026); Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, About Us and Constitution Order, 15 November 1983 (consulted 16 November 2026); Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, What to Do in an Emergency, sections on nuclear emergency and protective actions (consulted 16 November 2026); AERB Safety Guide, Criteria for Planning, Preparedness and Response for Nuclear or Radiological Emergency, AERB/NRF/SG/EP-5 (Rev. 1), sections 2.3–2.5.]

body:
Why accident studies matter

Serious nuclear accidents reveal how equipment conditions, human decisions and external hazards can combine. They are important because nuclear safety depends not only on preventing the initial fault but also on avoiding further failures when the plant is already under stress.

Three accidents are especially useful for understanding the development of modern nuclear-safety practice: Three Mile Island in 1979, Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima Daiichi in 2011. Their initiating conditions and consequences were different.

Three Mile Island, United States, 28 March 1979

At Three Mile Island Unit 2 in Pennsylvania, equipment malfunctions and difficulties interpreting the condition of the cooling system contributed to inadequate cooling and a partial melting of the reactor core. A relief valve remained open, and operators did not correctly recognize the loss of coolant in time. Radioactive material was largely contained, and releases beyond the plant were limited compared with later major accidents.

The accident demonstrated that safety systems and trained operators must work together. Clear instrument indications, reliable information about component conditions, realistic training, emergency procedures and effective communication are important safeguards.

Three Mile Island: The central lesson was that equipment faults can become severe when operators misunderstand the actual plant condition.

Chernobyl, then Soviet Union, 26 April 1986

The accident at Chernobyl Unit 4, in present-day Ukraine, occurred during an improperly conducted safety-related test. Serious reactor-design weaknesses combined with unsafe operating decisions. A rapid and uncontrolled power increase destroyed the reactor, followed by a fire and major releases of radioactive material into the environment.

Chernobyl highlighted the importance of a reactor design that does not become dangerously unstable under foreseeable conditions. It also demonstrated the need for independent protective arrangements, strict operating rules, transparent communication, effective regulation and a culture in which unsafe decisions are challenged.

The accident's consequences should not be attributed only to operator error or only to design flaws. Both contributed, and the weaknesses interacted.

Fukushima Daiichi, Japan, 11 March 2011

A major earthquake caused the operating reactors at Fukushima Daiichi to shut down automatically. The subsequent tsunami flooded and disabled important electrical and cooling equipment. With insufficient means to remove decay heat, severe core damage occurred in several units, accompanied by significant radioactive releases.

Fukushima demonstrated that even when the shutdown function succeeds, the cooling function can fail. It also showed that several backup systems may be lost together when they face a common external hazard, such as extensive flooding.

Important lessons include reassessing extreme natural hazards, protecting backup power and cooling equipment from common-cause damage, maintaining emergency capabilities when normal infrastructure fails and preparing for accidents affecting more than 1 unit.

Comparing the accidents correctly

All 3 accidents involved serious challenges to safe operation, but their mechanisms were not identical. Three Mile Island involved inadequate cooling aggravated by equipment and operator-information problems. Chernobyl involved a destructive uncontrolled power excursion associated with design and operating weaknesses. Fukushima involved an external natural disaster that disabled essential power and cooling arrangements after shutdown.

The general lesson is that a plant must be prepared not only for the most likely failure but also for combinations of failures and conditions that threaten several defences at once.

Prelims focus

  • Three Mile Island: United States, 28 March 1979, partial core meltdown.
  • Chernobyl: then Soviet Union, 26 April 1986, destructive power excursion and major radioactive release.
  • Fukushima Daiichi: Japan, 11 March 2011, earthquake and tsunami followed by loss of essential cooling.
  • Three Mile Island emphasizes instrument interpretation and operator response.
  • Fukushima emphasizes external hazards, common-cause failures and decay-heat removal.
  • Trap: Fukushima's operating reactors initially shut down; the subsequent inability to cool the fuel was crucial to the accident.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, section 16.5, Radioactive Wastes; IAEA International Nuclear Information System, Accident at the Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Station, 1980 record (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA International Nuclear Information System, The Chernobyl Reactor: Design Features and Reasons for Accident, 2016 record (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA International Nuclear Information System, International Fact Finding Expert Mission of the Fukushima Dai-Ichi NPP Accident, mission report, 2011 (consulted 16 November 2026); IAEA Incident and Emergency Centre, Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 event report, event date 11 March 2011 (consulted 16 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Three different initiating conditions revealed different weaknesses in nuclear safety.

title: Major Nuclear Accidents and the Safety Lessons They Teach

body:
What is radioactive waste?

Radioactive waste is material containing or contaminated with radionuclides for which no further use is foreseen and which is controlled as waste under the applicable regulatory system. It is not limited to material removed from nuclear reactors.

Radioactive waste may arise from nuclear power generation, fuel processing, research laboratories, medical diagnosis and treatment, industrial applications and the dismantling of nuclear facilities. It may occur as a solid, liquid or gas. Examples include contaminated protective clothing, filters, equipment, ion-exchange materials and residues from fuel processing.

Not all waste has the same hazard. A lightly contaminated item may require controlled management for a comparatively short time, while certain highly radioactive materials require isolation for much longer periods.

Radioactivity, half-life and long-term hazard

The radioactive half-life of a radionuclide is the time required for half of its radioactive nuclei to decay. After 1 half-life, 50% of the original radioactive nuclei remain; after 2 half-lives, 25% remain; after 3 half-lives, 12.5% remain.

For a single radionuclide in an unchanged quantity of material, the activity decreases in the same proportions as its undecayed nuclei. Actual waste often contains a mixture of radionuclides with different half-lives, so its total activity does not always follow 1 simple halving pattern.

Half-life alone does not determine danger. Waste classification also considers the amount and concentration of activity, the types of radiation emitted, the persistence of the radionuclides, possible exposure routes and whether the material produces significant decay heat.

The IAEA's 6 broad waste classes

The International Atomic Energy Agency describes 6 broad classes of radioactive waste. The system helps match the hazard and longevity of waste to appropriate management and disposal arrangements.

ClassMain characteristicTypical management approach
Exempt waste (EW)Meets applicable exemption or clearance criteriaCan leave regulatory control when the relevant conditions are satisfied.
Very short lived waste (VSLW)Contains radionuclides that decay sufficiently over a relatively short periodControlled storage for decay, followed by approved clearance where criteria are met.
Very low level waste (VLLW)Low activity concentration; relatively limited isolation needsAppropriate near-surface landfill-type disposal facilities with regulatory controls.
Low level waste (LLW)Above clearance levels, with limited quantities of long-lived radionuclidesEngineered near-surface disposal with containment and control.
Intermediate level waste (ILW)Requires greater isolation, particularly because of long-lived radionuclides; little or no heat removal requirementDisposal at appropriate intermediate or greater depth, depending on the waste and national safety requirements.
High level waste (HLW)Activity concentrations high enough to generate significant decay heat, or large amounts of long-lived radionuclides requiring the containment and isolation provided by deep geological disposalCooling and secure storage followed by deep geological disposal arrangements.

Understanding the differences

Very short lived and very low level describe different properties. VSLW is identified mainly by the short period over which its radionuclides decay to levels that may permit clearance. VLLW is identified by its relatively low activity concentration and limited isolation requirements. A waste item cannot be classified merely by observing that its physical quantity is small.

Low level does not mean completely harmless. LLW still requires appropriate containment, authorization and a suitable disposal route. Similarly, intermediate level does not necessarily imply substantial decay heat. The greater need for isolation may result from the amount of long-lived radionuclides present.

Spent nuclear fuel requires careful terminology. Where a country regards spent fuel as having no further use and intends to dispose of it, it is managed as high level waste. Where spent fuel is intended for reprocessing and recovery of useful nuclear material, its management status and subsequent waste streams differ.

The 6 classes are an international reference scheme. Individual countries may use their own detailed waste categories and acceptance criteria; an international class name should not automatically be treated as the exact legal category used at every Indian facility.

Prelims focus

  • The IAEA reference classification contains 6 classes: EW, VSLW, VLLW, LLW, ILW and HLW.
  • VSLW is commonly managed by controlled storage until sufficient radioactive decay has occurred.
  • LLW is generally suitable for appropriately engineered near-surface disposal.
  • ILW requires more isolation than LLW but little or no provision for decay-heat removal.
  • HLW may require substantial cooling and long-term geological isolation.
  • Trap: Waste classification depends on more than half-life or physical volume alone.

[Sources: IAEA, Use of a Graded Approach in the Application of the Management System Requirements for Facilities and Activities, IAEA-TECDOC-1740 (2014), Annex VIII, Table VIII-1, Classes of Radioactive Waste; IAEA, nuclear infrastructure learning-module Glossary, entries for Very Short Lived Waste, Very Low Level Waste and Vitrification (consulted 16 November 2026); NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, section 16.5, Radioactive Wastes; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Radioactive Waste Management: Indian Scenario, waste-origin and management sections (consulted 16 November 2026).]
